vanilla.note: Southern/lowland limit: warmest month below about 21.5 °C (boreal and montane). Generic vanilla spruce-like conifer: regional fir AND spruce analogues (spruce dominates most of the boreal and hemiboreal zone); not a species-identifiable leaf block.
Generic vanilla larch represents several regional species.
Correct vanilla hot-desert temperature setting for the mountain bristlecone analogue.
WCVP includes B. pendula subsp. mandshurica (Alaska birch, B. neoalaskana) in boreal North America; its Argentina South record is excluded as an error.
Vanilla limits river birch to 0-40% of the world height (sea level is 43%), i.e. to the lowest wet ground; kept as in vanilla, so it is rare.
Arctic-alpine shrub: tundra, mountains and northern mires; vanilla allows it up to 12 °C, which covered hemiboreal forest floors.
Northern limit about 60-61 °N in Finland and Russia (warmest month about 16.5 °C); WCVP botanical countries Finland and Russia North extend far beyond it.
Northern limit about 61-62 °N. Vanilla limits Norway maple to 0-40% of the world height, below sea level (43%); Earth uses its native range and temperature instead.
Cultivar; retain player planting, exclude natural historical forests.
Generic flat-topped acacia represented by umbrella thorn.
Generic ebony covers regional timber species; vanilla places it in the dry tropics, so the savanna ebony (jackalberry) is included and the rainforest species rarely qualifies.
Generic purpleheart covers regional Peltogyne timber species.
Coastal redwood; narrow coastal envelope further restricts botanical states.
Mediterranean cypress analogue; ornamental columnar form is not a separate wild species.
Generic bamboo proxy; vanilla has no botanical species identity.
Generic tree fern uses native Australasian analogues.

wildcrafttree.note: Generic stone pine ('cedar'): Siberian, Swiss and Korean stone pines.
Generic true fir: regional Abies species.
Generic spruce: regional Picea species. Wildcraft registers it at weight 2 beside vanilla's fir (100); Earth uses it as the regional spruce next to the generic fir (weight x8).
Generic elm: European (wych, European white, field), North American (American, slippery) and Asian (Siberian, Japanese) elms.

Generic beech: European, Oriental, American and Japanese beech. Wildcraft registers it at weight 1.7; beech dominates natural central European forest, so Earth scales it x12 (about English oak's weight).
Generic white birch: downy birch (Eurasia) and paper birch (North America).
Tree alders: black and grey alder (Europe to Siberia), red alder (Pacific North America), Manchurian and Japanese alder, Italian alder.
Shrub alders: green alder (circumboreal mountains), grey/speckled alder thickets, hazel alder.
Tree willows: white, goat and bay willow.
Shrub willows of Eurasia and boreal North America.
Ornamental form excluded from natural historical forests.
Beach and littoral forest tree; WCVP countries such as Borneo or Kenya are otherwise far larger than its habitat.
Wildcraft's eucalyptus is the rainbow eucalyptus (Mindanao to New Guinea), not an Australian gum; Australian eucalypts come from Floral Zones and the ghost gum.
Generic linden: small- and large-leaved lime, Amur linden, American basswood.
Generic ash: European, narrow-leaved, white, green and Manchurian ash.

alnusglutinosa.note: Black alder: floodplains, lake shores and fens. Floral Zones' tree is large (size x1.8), so on upland sites it dominated the canopy.

alnusalnobetula.note: Green alder: subalpine (Alps, Carpathians) and boreal shrub, not lowland temperate forest.

alnusalnobetulashrub.note: Green alder: subalpine (Alps, Carpathians) and boreal shrub, not lowland temperate forest.

quercuspetraea.note: Sessile oak needs mild winters (oceanic to sub-oceanic Europe; absent from the continental Baltic interior and the north).

lysilomalatisiliquum.note: Frost-tender: South Florida, the Keys and the Caribbean, not central Florida.

roystonearegia.note: Frost-tender royal palm: South Florida and the Caribbean.

exclusions.note: WCVP lists silver birch as native in Argentina South (distribution record 1105526); it is introduced in South America. Without this exclusion Patagonia's forests became 100% silver birch.

chorology.note: Natural ranges finer than a botanical country, from Caudullo, Welk and San-Miguel-Ayanz 2017 (European woody species, CC BY 4.0): every native polygon and isolated-population point of the species folder, subspecies included, introduced (syn) layers left out. A WCVP region of a mapped taxon then holds the tree only inside that taxon's map, widened by one grid cell. Species that people had spread well beyond the mapped range by 1318 keep their WCVP regions alone.

exclude.Juglans regia: walnut was planted across Europe since Roman times
exclude.Cupressus sempervirens: planted around the Mediterranean since antiquity
exclude.Laurus nobilis: grown around the Mediterranean since antiquity
exclude.Taxus baccata: yew grew through Europe's woods until the longbow-stave trade of the 14th to 16th centuries cut it out of much of its range; today's scattered stands are what is left

Pinus sylvestris.note: Caledonian pinewood still grew in glens across the Highlands in 1318; the mapped native stands are the remnants, about one per cent of it (box: south, north, west, east)

analogues.name: humid tropical forest
analogues.note: Stand-ins where no or few installed native species qualify (e.g. the Congo basin, West Africa, India, Borneo's interior): kapok for the emergent canopy (Ceiba is pantropical in cultivation), purpleheart for tropical hardwoods, bamboo and tree ferns.

analogues.name: dry tropical woodland and savanna
analogues.note: Flat-topped acacia and ebony (jackalberry-like) for savanna and dry forest; kapok for seasonal forest.

analogues.name: subtropical savanna and dry woodland
analogues.note: Summer-rain savanna and thorn woodland outside the tropics (South African Highveld, Chaco edges, inland Australia): acacia and ebony only, never temperate trees.

analogues.name: tropical montane forest (Americas, Asia, Pacific)
analogues.note: Cloud and montane forest (Andes, Central America, Malesia, New Guinea, Hawaii): oak for montane broadleaf trees (real oaks in Central America, Colombia and South-East Asia), the generic conifer for podocarps, tree ferns.

analogues.name: Afromontane forest
analogues.note: Ethiopian, East African, Madagascan and South African montane forest: the generic conifer for podocarps and junipers, tree ferns, Floral Zones' Afrocarpus where installed. No oaks (none are native south of the Sahara).

analogues.name: subtropical humid forest of South America
analogues.note: Atlantic Forest, Parana pine forest, Paraguay, Uruguay and north-eastern Argentina: oak for laurel/broadleaf forest, kapok for silk-floss trees (Ceiba speciosa), the Norfolk Island pine for the Parana pine (Araucaria angustifolia), jacaranda, tree ferns.

analogues.name: subtropical humid forest
analogues.note: Humid subtropics outside South America and Africa (Florida and the Gulf coast, southern China, Japan, eastern Australia): oak for live/laurel oaks and evergreen broadleaf trees, the pine for southern pines, bamboo and tree ferns.

analogues.name: subtropical humid forest of southern Africa
analogues.note: Coastal and scarp forest of south-eastern Africa: tree ferns, the generic conifer for yellowwoods (Podocarpus), Floral Zones' Afrocarpus and stinkwood where installed, ebony.

analogues.name: Mediterranean woodland
analogues.note: Summer-dry sclerophyll woodland (central Chile, the Cape, south-western and southern Australia, Mediterranean gaps): oak for evergreen oaks and sclerophyll trees, cypress, pine; holm oak and Aleppo pine when Floral Zones is installed.

analogues.name: southern temperate rainforest
analogues.note: Valdivian and Patagonian forest, Tasmania, New Zealand: oak (or Wildcraft beech, or Floral Zones' silver beech when installed) for southern beech (Nothofagus), the generic conifer for southern conifers, tree ferns.

analogues.name: northern boreal and subarctic woodland
analogues.note: Northern gaps without an installed native tree (Iceland, the Faroes, Kamchatka with vanilla only): birch woodland with some conifers.

analogues.name: northern temperate forest
analogues.note: Northern temperate gaps: Earth's forest-type mix of oak, maple, birch, the generic fir and pine.
